final_answer: No. The trial court did not err; the disqualification order should stand (and mandamus relief would be denied). Under Texas law, which governs a Dallas state-court disqualification motion, a nonlawyer (legal assistant or paralegal) who worked on a matter for one side and later works on the same matter for opposing counsel triggers a two-step presumption framework. First, because Jones actually worked on the Apex-Prestige suit at Owens Farmer (drafting litigation documents, hundreds of privileged communications, strategy meetings), it is conclusively (irrebuttably) presumed that she obtained Apex's confidences. Second, there is a presumption that she shared those confidences with her new firm, Smith Fullingham. For nonlawyers that second presumption is rebuttable, but only through prophylactic measures, not by denials of disclosure: the firm must have admonished/instructed the nonlawyer not to work on the matter and taken formal, institutionalized screening measures that make access to confidences remote (In re Columbia Valley Healthcare System, 320 S.W.3d 819 (Tex. 2010); In re Guaranty Insurance Services, 343 S.W.3d 130 (Tex. 2011)). Here the firm did nothing when she was hired in 2017, did not ask about her prior work, did not instruct her to stay off the matter, and had her work on the very matter on thirteen occasions and e-file two documents in March 2022 under the firm's direction. Her professed lack of memory and the firm's assurance that she shared nothing are legally irrelevant because the presumption is not overcome by denials. Screening announced only in 2023, after Apex discovered the problem, is too late; where the nonlawyer has already worked on the matter at the firm's direction, the Columbia Valley irrebuttable presumption of sharing applies and disqualification is required. The facts track In re Zaidi (Tex. Apr. 10, 2026) (No. 24-0245), where the Supreme Court of Texas, on near-identical facts (a legal assistant who previously worked for the opposing party's former counsel, later performed intermittent secretarial work on the same case for the defendants' firm without being admonished, and filed documents), denied mandamus and upheld disqualification, holding that the employee must be admonished before commencing work on a later-arising conflict, regardless of whether she was switching sides when hired, and that late screening does not cure. Waiver: Disqualification can be waived by unreasonable delay, but the movant bears the burden of showing waiver by delay (In re EPIC Holdings, 985 S.W.2d 41 (Tex. 1998) general principle, not independently verified in this run). Apex moved within about two months of actually discovering Jones's involvement in January 2023; per Zaidi, receipt of e-filing notifications bearing the assistant's name does not conclusively establish waiver or knowledge, and Apex's inquiry and short investigation was reasonable. The 2017-2022 period of non-knowledge does not count against Apex because the firm never disclosed her and filing notices did not give notice of her prior connection. Also relevant: disqualification is a severe remedy requiring the movant to show actual prejudice, but under the nonlawyer rule the presumption supplies that showing. Caveats: I could not retrieve the full text of Zaidi or Columbia Valley (the sites were blocked), so the Zaidi holdings are drawn from search-result summaries of the opinion, and the same-matter and screening points were verified only via secondary summaries; pin cites and the EPIC waiver standard are unverified.

authorities.proposition: Irrebuttable presumption nonlawyer who worked on matter obtained confidences; firm avoids disqualification only by instructing assistant not to work on matter and taking reasonable shielding steps; if assistant works on matter at firm's direction, disqualification required.

authorities.proposition: Nonlawyer must be admonished before commencing work on a later-arising conflict to avoid disqualification; e-filing notifications do not conclusively establish waiver; mandamus denied, disqualification upheld; denials of disclosure do not overcome presumption.

claims.text: Texas applies an irrebuttable presumption that Jones obtained Apex's confidences and a presumption of sharing with Smith Fullingham that is rebuttable only by prophylactic admonishment/screening.
Smith Fullingham failed to admonish or screen Jones before she worked on the matter, and post-discovery screening does not cure, so disqualification was proper.
Apex did not waive by delay: e-filing notices do not conclusively establish waiver and it moved within about two months of discovering the conflict.
